utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Zecevic, continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before I start, I have another 15 minutes maximum of cross-examination, but one thing, the matter came up yesterday, when I talked to my client. Actually, my client was asking me what is the difference between the direct evidence versus indirect evidence against him, and I would like guidance by this Honourable Trial Chamber in this respect, because my client heard that we were talking about direct and indirect evidence, and I would like to know what is the position of this Honourable Trial Chamber in this respect so I can tell that to my client in order that I preserve that he knowingly waives his right to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that will be dealt with later, if we can finish the cross-examination of Mr. Tihic, because that was not the basis of his asking for rest today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I understand completely. But we were talking about his absence on previous occasions, Your Honours, in that case, I will have just for the record, I will have to object before I -- object on this before I inform my client about the indirect versus direct definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think you should worry about that because the Trial Chamber is equally concerned about his rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And about not undermining his rights in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fact, there are so many things we are trying to do with the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To try to make it possible for him to be in the courtroom as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because we wouldn't like his health to break down because that means we can't go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We neither, but at the same time we have the obligation to preserve the best interests of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. So we will deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: (Witness answered through interpreter)

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, yesterday afternoon, we finished by discussing a document that you were unable to identify, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher's assistance. [In English] And I'd like D9/2 ter. If you can show the original to the witness and the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the contents, roughly, of this, that although the document appears to me to be a little -- there's no stamp, there's no signature, but I do remember the contents and I do remember telling my secretary to compile something like this. But as a rule, the document had to have a letterhead, the proper letterhead, and a stamp, and usually a signature. But, as I say, I called up my secretary and told her to write a certificate of this kind. Although, as I say, I don't know if it's authentic, because there's no logo, letterhead, and stamp, but I do recall the contents and I do remember telling her to write something along those lines. So what I'm saying is I can't authenticate the document, but I do remember saying that something along these lines should be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, what you're saying is that you issued orders to your secretary to write a document with the following contents.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So as far as the contents in this document, that is not being contested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, Mr. Tihic: The signatory is the SDA Municipal Board, Bosanski Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there should have been the party emblem first and then it should say "the President" usually. But yes, it does say "SDA Municipal Board, Bosanski Samac." You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know Fuad Jasenica, do you not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Ibrahim Salkic, you also know him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he was a member of the SDA, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Tihic: What kind of equipment are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two of them, or one of them -- I think Fuad came and said that he had a connection of some kind in Croatia and that he could procure some weapons but that he would need a certificate to prove that he was there on behalf of someone, that he had been sent on someone's behalf. And first of all, I was a little doubtful whether I should issue a certificate of this kind, because Fuad was a young man; he was a taxi driver; he didn't hold a post, position of any kind. But in view of the situation that prevailed in Samac at the time, everybody had weapons, especially the Serbs. They had a lot. We didn't have much. But I said, "Well, let me write a certificate. Perhaps something will come of it." Not much time went by, perhaps a day or two, and I received information that they had brought in, I think, 50 automatic rifles, and I told them to take them off to the Territorial Defence headquarters in Bosanski Samac, which had been set up two or three days prior to that. So that those weapons were taken there straight away, and I assume that they were distributed later on, in part at least. Perhaps something had remained. That's as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Tihic: If you recall, were those weapons from Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Croatia, probably Slavonski Brod or Djakovo. I can't remember which.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your book, you write that there were 50 automatic rifles, 2 mortars, a few Zolja rocket launchers and some ammunition.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on the Chief of Staff informed me of the contents, and if I wrote that down, then that's what it probably was. But it was handed over to the TO, to their warehouse, and they made a list of it. They registered and recorded what had been handed over to them. That's what I was told, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tihic: You mentioned having given orders to your secretary to type out a certificate with these contents. Do you allow for the possibility that the document you have in front of you is actually the copy that was kept in the archive, a copy of that original document which was later stored in the archive?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I can't be sure, because I would have had to sign a certificate of this kind. It was a serious certificate and it would have had to have been signed. Now, this isn't. This piece of paper isn't signed. But as I say, I don't challenge the contents, but whether that is the actual piece of paper and certificate, I don't know, because they're not -- it's not logical that it doesn't have a letterhead, a logo, it doesn't say "the President" at the bottom, and it hasn't got a signature. So possibly, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you: Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Mr. Tihic: The original copy of that certificate was, I suppose, handed over to Suad [as interpreted] Jasenica and Ibrahim Salkic for them to be able to pick up the weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I heard from them later on, they didn't actually need the certificate, so they didn't hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it was probably given to them, handed over to them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that it was given to them, because they had asked for it, but they said that it served no purpose and they didn't need it after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Tihic: Do you know why Fuad Jasenica came to you to ask for a certificate and not the chief of the TO? Because, as you say, the TO had been established three days prior to his coming to ask you for the certificate.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when he actually asked me for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says the 14th of April on the certificate.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether the TO had been established then, I'm not sure, but if it was the 14th, then, yes, I think the TO had been set up. I don't know why he asked me before he asked the TO headquarters. Perhaps he didn't know that the TO headquarters had in fact been established at that particular moment because it hadn't perhaps been publicly announced yet. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like, Your Honours, to move this document into evidence, because if the Prosecutor is not objecting, since the witness has certified about the contents of the document -- testified about the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me hear the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. They had ID numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, D9/2 ter. And there is an unofficial translation. When the document is translated by the official translators, then we will provide the registry with the English -- official English translation whenever it's going to be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number formally pronounced, please, as exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D9/2 ter and D9/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please take a look at the document you were looking at yesterday, with respect to Hasan Bicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the usher's assistance to hand [In English] D3/2 ter ID, the document which was handed to the witness yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. Tihic, the document you have before you, and the document you looked at a moment ago related to Fuad Jasenica and Ibrahim Salkic, they are similar in content, are they not, the two documents?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are partially similar, but the form of the two documents differ considerably. Here it says, "President." There it says, "Municipal Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the contents, not the form. Are they similar in content? They are, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tihic, please, I assume you had somebody who replaced you when you were not present yourself in Bosanski Samac, when you were away somewhere, I mean within the party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did officially have a deputy, but I was in Samac all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And who was that, may I ask you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Izet Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see, Izet Izetbegovic. So do you allow for the possibility that somebody else from the party might have compiled this certificate for Hasan Bicic, the one you're looking at now, the one you have before you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's asking for strictly speculation now. "Is it possible somebody else could have done this and put this document under my name?" We would object at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And tell me, please, Mr. Tihic, typing out documents of this kind, the typing was done by your secretary, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us her name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name was Hata Baraktavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see, Hata with an "H," Hata Baraktavic. Do you know where we could find the lady now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, she lives in Zagreb somewhere. She's married and lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The next counsel? This is counsel for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tihic. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and I am an attorney and Defence counsel for Mr. Tadic, and in that capacity I shall be asking you a few questions. I'm going to try and ask you -- put the questions to you so that you can give a yes or no answer. If you're not certain or don't know, please say so. If we need to get an explanation in addition to your answer to the question, then we can do so, but the Prosecution can ask you again if they feel any clarifications are required. So those are my instructions to you so that we can move as quickly as possible. Mr. Tihic, as far as I understood in the questions you have given so far -- in the answers you've given so far, you lived quite near to the AS Cafe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to work, you had to pass by the AS Cafe, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever drop by into the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period immediately prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps twice, yes. I would go in from time to time, once, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the members of all ethnic groups used to frequent the cafe? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which means, Mr. Omer Nalic, for example?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the names, but I do know that everybody would frequent the cafe and when I was there on the few occasions, yes, Bosniaks, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So it was a normal type of cafe, the kind that existed in Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, in a statement by you a month ago, you said that you met members of the JNA and 4th Detachment on a number of occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you would meet them in the company of Mr. Izetbegovic and other political and party functionaries, whether they were alone, whether -- but you had several meetings as far as I understood?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Among the others, you mentioned your meetings and talks with Colonel Nikolic and Colonel Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And with Simo Zaric, Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May we take it, then, that with those JNA representatives and 4th Detachment representatives, you never had an official meeting in the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, can we take it that your associates, as far as you were aware, had no official meetings either with the representatives of the 4th Detachment and the JNA in the AS Cafe?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, let's move on to another topic now. In your previous statements before this -- and testimony before this Tribunal, you mentioned that you were a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that within the frameworks of local party, Communist Party organisation, you held certain posts. Were you a member of the Presidency - let me be specific - of the basic organisation of the League of Communists of Samac at a given time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about some Executive Council boards, something like that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in what was called the District Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was thinking of. And it was the fourth local party organisation in Samac. You previously said that you think that Miroslav Tadic had been a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody was. Those were the times. Everybody, practically everybody, was a member of the League of Communists, and that's why I said that Tadic was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that within the framework of the party, the League of Communists, and the functions you had, that you met Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. He was at the school, and I was in the local party organisation. I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember that earlier, before the war, legal proceedings were undertaken to have him sent away from the school where he was a teacher because he was not a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Discharge him from his post at the school. Do you happen to know that when the multi-party system was introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina and when it was implemented in Samac, whether he was a member of any of the parties that had been established in Bosanski Samac? I'm referring to Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I'm going to focus on your arrest and the time you spent in detention now. You were arrested on a Saturday, which was the 18th of April, and you were taken to the premises of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From there, you were transferred to the TO warehouse, opposite the SUP building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that a whole group of detainees, together with you, were transferred from the SUP building to the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted], two Bicic brothers were transferred with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And who else was there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the four of us. The four of us were transferred. We were in a room and we were transferred to the TO warehouse, where we encountered a lot of people, 40 or 50 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Ibrahim Salkic? Was he transferred with you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was just in the room with us, up on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But he was in the TO?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived, Salkic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Lukac and Izet Izetbegovic were brought in later on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were all put up together in the TO warehouse prior to being transferred to Brcko on the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the TO warehouse for two or three days and then I was in a cell in the police building, police station. I was there all the time. I slept in the cell. After I was taken from the TO headquarters for my first interview and interrogation, they didn't take me back. They put me up in a cell. There were nine of us in this cell, which was one metre by a metre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were in the cell, you say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were nine of us. It was a very small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were in the TO, there was one room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a big room, a large room, 15 by 15 or 20 metres. That was the size of that hall. And there were 50 or 60 of us there. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you testified on the 19th of September, 2001, before this Tribunal, and you said, in response to a question from the Prosecutor, although you weren't quite certain, that you think you had seen Miroslav Tadic going into the TO premises where you were incarcerated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, take a moment to recollect. The four witnesses said that they did not see Miroslav Tadic, they did not see him going in. I'm thinking of the brothers Bicic, Ibrahim Salkic. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, what can that question do but invite this witness to speculate as to what the other witnesses said? That's the whole purpose of it. There can be no other purpose. This witness has got his position; they've got theirs. What's the point of putting theirs to him? What's he supposed to say: "They're right," "They're wrong," "I don't know"? But he's being asked, basically, to delve into their minds, explain their answers, explain their position, and he can't do that. He can only explain his. And so for that reason, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to ask us to clarify one point. In front of this same Tribunal, in this same trial, on the 18th of October, during the course of the cross-examination by Mr. Pantelic of Mr. Izetbegovic with respect to the trunk that was in the helicopter, he wanted to show the statements of Lukac and Tihic, and my colleague, Mr. di Fazio, opposed this. However, Judge Singh, on page -- with respect to that request, he allowed Mr. Pantelic to be shown that testimony. And when we are ascertaining facts in this Court, the witnesses present their views and state the facts and we show them evidence, and Mr. Zecevic showed a document to the witness. So testimony by witnesses in this Court is also evidence. Now, I don't see the reason why, if a witness is not certain and says he thinks, why can we not present the statements of other witnesses as evidence? Because it was brought out during the trial in this Court. That's what we do in my legal system. And on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please. And can one of you sit down? I'm wondering what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the same topic, the same question, in the cross-examination, we were faced with a situation where we could show witness testimonies of Prosecution witnesses, and it was precisely Mr. Lukac and Tihic with respect to the cross-examination of Mr. Izetbegovic. And now we have the same situation, and the witness has said that he thinks he came. So it is witness testimony which is evidence, and therefore, witness testimony of this kind, whether in a direct form, by reading out the sentence, by showing the witness the actual sentence or asking him in some different way, by describing what the witness had said -- may I do this? We have a public trial here. All the trials are on the Internet. And now we are not allowed to ascertain the truth, to attempt to ascertain the truth. And it is precisely through questions of this kind that we don't wish to play hide and seek. We wish to place all our cards on the table. I know that the Trial Chamber will see what value it's going to attach, what probative value, but we can clarify a fact and not have to leave it in the air and leave it for further appraisal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel, the procedure in this Tribunal, as far as witnesses are concerned, whether they belong to the Defence or to the Prosecution, is that you challenge the witness with his own evidence, at whatever stage that evidence was taken, or the contents of a statement anywhere, relevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber. The other point is that when you want to challenge a witness with the evidence of some other witness, you don't say to the witness: The evidence of so-and-so was like this. You ask it -- you put it to him as a question. So you don't -- yes. You don't make the witness describe the other witness. You don't move the witness to describe the other witness as perhaps having told a lie or not having observed correctly or whatever. You simply say to him, "There is evidence to the effect that ... What do you say to that?" All right? And then in the closing arguments, that's when you now pick it up, right, the contradictions. Then you use them to water down the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have fully understood that. It's quite clear to me, the role of the Defence and the role of all the parties, notably, the role of the Trial Chamber in evaluating all evidence presented. However, I thought that if the Prosecutor can be allowed to show a witness statement from a previous trial or previous proceedings in order to refresh someone's memory, why can't we do the same thing in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think that was ever done. It was statements -- if I thought that was done, it must have been statements of the same witness. If, at all, a transcript is shown to a witness, it must be a transcript that has already been placed on record. Or that is going to be placed on record. For instance, I can't remember that having been done. May I ask the Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: It was. It was the same witness's statement. I wasn't providing a statement of another witness to that witness, whoever it was. I can't recall which particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I recall. MR. DI FAZIO: It was definitely that witness's own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And like I said, you pick out what the contradiction is and you put it to the witness as a question. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. We are going to rephrase our question now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, while you were at the TO, from the place where you were, could you always see people entering the room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to get up when somebody entered the room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first days, when they would tell us to get up, we'd get up, but I do not recall us getting up automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You described the beatings at the Territorial Defence in detail in your statement, who beat who and who was beaten, that is to say that that could be seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: These beatings could be seen quite clearly by the others as well, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Like the Bicic brothers, Ibrahim Salkic, everybody else who was there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the local Serbs walked into the TO. I'm not referring to the Serbs who beat you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At what time of day did they come in, these local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All day. I don't know exactly, the morning, in the afternoon, I can't say. They would walk in at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP in September and October 1994, that it seemed to you that you were forgetting things so you wrote down the names and events that you remember. Are those your memories?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In these memories, recollections, you never mentioned Miroslav Tadic walking into the TO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was important. That's probably why I didn't write it down. But Miroslav did go into the TO headquarters. I remember that now. I remember some of the details. I can even explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the nickname Brko means in our language?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brko is a person who wears a mustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that the nickname Brko means a person who wears a mustache?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that was Tadic's nickname also, that they called him Miro Brko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in October, and September, 1994, when you describe Miroslav Tadic, you refer to him as Miroslav Tadic and Miro Brko, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. May I confer just briefly with my co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, do you remember the time of the day when Tadic walked into the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think it was daytime. I don't know exactly which time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So it was daytime?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me it was daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to show the witness his statement now, the one given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 22nd and 23rd of September, 1994, and the 31st of October, 1994. MR. DI FAZIO: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be clear, Defence counsel. Those dates, 22nd, 23rd September and 31st of October, are for one statement? MR. DI FAZIO: That's what I was about to explain. That's all the one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly for the interpreters this part that starts, "At 10.00 p.m.," and it ends by saying, "One man named Brko would come in."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 10.00 p.m. they took us out of the police station to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, to a warehouse across the street from the police station. There were about 50 people in the room. The other men gave us some paper to put on the floor to sleep on, but they forced us to sing Chetnik songs so no one could sleep. The guards forced us to make a chorus and sing. Then they would take people and beat them and they would make another chorus and beat people some more. One man named 'Brko' came in."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the statement any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you still assert that it was daytime or was it like you put it in your statement to the OTP that it was after 10.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it was in the evening, and possibly it was on the next day as well. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't object to the direction that my learned friend is going in. It's quite proper, I submit. But unless I'm wrong, the witness hasn't said that this is the same Brko. It may or may not be, I don't know, but until that's established and clear, we don't know if there is any sort of inconsistency in the statement and his evidence. So that should be done first before we proceed to this part to this final question, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the Defence counsel has understood what the Prosecution is trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As for this nickname Brko, it's the usual nickname for people who wear a mustache; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that everybody has this nickname but Miro Brko did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was there another Brko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think that in that context it is Miro Brko that is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In all these statements given to the OTP and before this Trial Chamber, you always say Miro Brko, and it is only this time that you said Brko, in the statement you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, that's the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that there was another Brko, a guard, somebody else who would come there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just referring to Miro Brko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Miroslav Tadic walk in on his own then?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he walked in with someone else. I'll tell you why I remember this particular event and I assert that it was him. I remember that he walked in and that he shook hands with some people, and that after he got out, those men in camouflage, whatever their name was, took -- came in and took some of these people out, and we thought -- and beat them. And Miro -- and we thought that this was a sign that Miro was giving to these people who administered the beatings, by shaking these people's hands. I don't know whether that really was a message that he was getting across to these people who would then come in and beat these people, but that is how I remember all of this, and that is why this event is so clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel has to put his question again. The interpreters cannot follow his speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, did you hear the -- the microphone is not on and the interpreters did ask that the question be put to the witness again, because they couldn't pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did he walk in by himself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He walked in with somebody else, either a member of the special forces or someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as far as I can remember, he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When he showed up, did you comment the fact that he appeared with Ibrahim Salkic, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who I commented upon this with. I was sitting in a corner with Gibic, Mersad, Ibrahim Salkic. We slept there together in a corner. Possibly with him, but I can't really remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Bicic, maybe?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in another -- another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Muhamed Bicic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I think you're putting the interpreter in distress as well. So please, there is no need to rush. Just pause after an answer and we can understand you better, and your question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you sat with Ibrahim Salkic, right? This is what I want to ask you. In the TO premises, in that corner of yours, as you put it, who was sitting with you, Ibrahim Salkic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrahim Salkic; Gibic, Mersad; [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how long did Miroslav Tadic stay there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, perhaps five minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who did he shake hands with?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names exactly but as soon as he walked in, then on the left-hand side, perhaps two or three men who were standing there, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you do not remember the names of the men that Miroslav Tadic shook hands with and who were allegedly beaten after he had left?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You thought that wasn't important -- it wasn't an important thing to remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To remember, no. It would have had to be over a thousand pages if I recorded all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, we're going to move on to a different topic now. You are a member of the Main Board of the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Hasan Cengic was Secretary-General of the Party of Democratic Action in one period of time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly he was, for a short while, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in February 1992, Hasan Cengic, at the meeting of the head committee of the SDA, suggested that the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be put under control of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Nihad Halibegovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the officials or, let's say, one of top people of the SDA in that period?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At city level, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Halibegovic, together with a group of his associates, established the first headquarters of the Patriotic League, the regional headquarters for Sarajevo, on the 31st of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Rusmir Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in April 1992, together with Alija Izetbegovic and Muhamed Cengic, he agreed to establish an organisation that could instigate a revolt of the Muslim people, and in that sense he had discussions with all generals of the JNA who were of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in such positions in the party then in order to be able to know that. It is possible, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present at a meeting at the police building in Sarajevo on the 10th of June, 1991, when the Council of National Defence of the Muslim People was established?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there. Izet Izetbegovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about what was discussed later, but I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that occasion a proclamation was issued where, under number 7, armed resistance was called for on the part of the entire JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at this same meeting a Council for National Defence was established with 12 members?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of a certain Senad Memic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Senad Memic was given an assignment by the SDA leadership to organise the transport of weapons from Ljubljana to the B & H via Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that he did go through Samac and that we met on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the truck with the weapons that Memic was driving broke down in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then, when the weapons were being reloaded into the kombi van of the veterinary station --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The truck. -- you got some of the weapons from this Memic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got 20 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. Now I know him. I knew him before as well. Now I know him more, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you read his book, "The Clever Strategy"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Sefer Halilovic was in charge of military affairs in the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, this is page 27, line 12. The transcript said: "Did you read his book, 'The Clever Strategy'?" It is not "clever." It's "The Cunning Strategy." So there's a big difference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that so, Counsel? The counsel cross-examining, is that the correct title?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the cunning/sly strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was not registered. Do you know that Sefer Halilovic was in charge of military affairs in the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that later. At that time I did not know who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that together with him you took part in the meeting of the Main Board of the SDA on Mount Igman in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Igman, but I don't know whether Sefer was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, was there a discussion on military matters, inter alia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not one of the main topics that was discussed. It was basically under "other business," "miscellaneous." People were saying, "So what are we going to do, President Izetbegovic? Should we be with the Croats? Should we take weapons?" There were questions like this that were raised, but then ultimately this was not one of the items on the agenda. It was really under "other business."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was Izet Izetbegovic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. We were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, during your previous testimony you described a series of meetings that start with the multi-party elections onwards until the conflict broke out, and you made an effort to work for a peaceful solution, to ease tensions in order to prevent an armed conflict from breaking out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This was your strategy, to put it that way, some kind of policy of yours?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there would not be a conflict, that nobody wanted a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that you all made an effort to ease tensions?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some more, others less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about your party.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were making an effort to ease tensions because we knew that we were the weakest in comparison to all other parties, that we did not have weapons, that this was in our interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, the statement of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the president of your party, that he gave and that reads as follows: "I would sacrifice peace for sovereign B & H, and for this peace in B & H, I would not sacrifice its sovereignty." Can we agree that this kind of statement did not contribute to an easing of tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a statement and if you take it out of context, you see, you can't really look at things that way. You cannot take things out of an entity and then say that that is what it means. You have to know what Izetbegovic said before that and what Izetbegovic said after that. Izetbegovic made every effort in order to prevent war from breaking out. He proposed a Federation. We Muslims, the SDA, were not bothered by Yugoslavia. Our interest was to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting you, but I just wanted to ask you about this particular statement, and later on you will have an opportunity to explain your own position. That's what has already been said to you. So it is in this context that I mention this and the context in which I put this question. Did this particular statement contribute to an easing of growing tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina? You can say, "No, it didn't," or "I don't know" or "I do not agree."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree, because you are putting things the wrong way. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I think we're rapidly descending into a political discussion here. I simply can't see the relevance of this. I haven't objected to any of the questions leading up to the various party machinations in respect of weapons and the existence of any sort of preparations relating to war and so on, but this now is, A, involving a dissertation on what President Izetbegovic said and is simply so distant from the issues in the indictment that it becomes now irrelevant, and that's the main basis of my objection to this question. What does it matter and how is it going to assist you as to whether or not President Izetbegovic's statements were appropriate at the time or not? And so for that reason, I submit that we shouldn't go down this road of an analysis of his pre-war position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the purpose of my question was that the witness, as a prominent political functionary and the president of the Party of Democratic Action now, who has already in previous testimonies given assessments and views of his political views, that he could give his own opinions; not speculation, just his own political opinion as to the tensions that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time immediately prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That he can do, but he cannot give -- ask the consequences of a statement made at a political rally. It is -- the way you asked the question is somehow asking him to speculate. You can only ask him, "After such a statement was made, what happened, what did you observe?" Because he is a fact witness. He is not a political analyst. MR. DI FAZIO: Indeed. If Your Honours look at the question, the question is this: "Did this particular statement, that of President Alija Izetbegovic, contribute to an easing of growing tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Precisely. MR. DI FAZIO: How is that going to assist you? If my learned friend wants to look into tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina insofar as they are linked to what happened in Bosanski Samac in the municipality, fine, I've got no problem with that, but whether or not Alija Izetbegovic's statement on this or that eased growing tensions is A, speculative, and B, really remote from the issues that we have to deal with. I don't see how it's going to assist us -- or the Chamber, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Like I said, the witness is not a political analyst. You can ask him as to what happened thereafter, because he's a fact witness. He can tell us whether or not there was peace. And there is relevance in the sense that we are trying also to look at statehood, in which case we may be examining who was actually in authority, was there law and order, who was in authority, who was in office, who was in power. There is some relevance. It's just the way -- MR. DI FAZIO: In that sense, yes, of course, that topic certainly. But whether or not what he said eased tensions or not doesn't really go to that question. But my broad objection is on the grounds of relevance, and I can see this rapidly descending into a quagmire of political discussion that's not going to assist the Chamber, and so on that basis, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure counsel has got the gist of the matters discussed by the prosecuting counsel, and we will avoid turning this into a political discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reformulate that question, in keeping with your guidance, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, after this statement by Mr. Izetbegovic, what happened in Bosanski Samac? Was there an easing of tensions? Did they cease? Did the members of the Muslim ethnic group cease to arm themselves, or what?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special happened, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the process of arming that the Muslim ethnic group undertook?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- it's debatable whether the Muslims did that or not, because the Muslims were the ones that armed themselves least. All the other sides had more weapons. You were able to see how many weapons we were able to procure. So that statement did not affect arms, whether they increased or decreased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May we then agree that after that statement, there was no easing of tensions, but that they escalated, the conflict escalated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, I am Aleksandar Lazarevic, an attorney, and on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Simo Zaric, I shall be asking questions in the cross-examination. However, before I start with my questions, I should like, on behalf of my client, to express his profound condolences and regrets for all the suffering and hardships and difficulties that you had to go through during your period of incarceration. Having said that, may I now proceed with the cross-examination, if you agree? Thank you. Mr. Tihic, I should like to go back to the year 1990. At that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was called the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was still a component part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May we agree now that at that time, on the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, federal -- the federal constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia prevailed, as well as federal laws? They were in force on the territory of the republic, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to ask for the assistance of Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are some sentences of the federal constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia. I don't believe that it is necessary to tender them as evidence because I believe that this full document will be tendered to the Court through our expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just for cross-examination of this witness, and I believe we just need some ID number, or maybe not, whatever you feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's usually safer to have an ID number for identification purposes only, if the document is discussed by the witness. I take it those are excerpts of the constitution which was in force then in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D11/4 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, would you take a look at the document? It is the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. I remember this book and what it looked like, the book of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would you now, slowly, to facilitate the work of the interpreters, read Article 237 of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The inalienable right and duty of the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia, the working people and citizens, is to protect and defend their independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and the constitution of the SFRY, and the social order of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. Do we agree that that is a constitutional provision, the fundamental rights and duties of protecting the country, the constitutional order and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you read Article 240, please, which has also been marked?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 240: "The armed forcers of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia defend the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and the social order ascertained by this constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are -- make up one entity and are composed of the Yugoslav People's Army as a joint armed force of all the nations and nationalities and all the working people and citizens of the country, and it is also composed of the Territorial Defence as the broadest form of organisation of an armed, all people's or total national defence, every citizen who, with arms, or in any other way, opposes attacks by members of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the armed forces of the SFRY are composed of the JNA and the TO and represent a whole, one unity? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you read Article 241, please? It is a short one.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The military obligation of citizens is general and all embracing."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that all military-able men, citizens, were duty-bound to perform their military assignments and responsibilities and obligations regardless of national, republican and religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law provides for that and defines it more specifically but, yes, that was the case. Perhaps there were some exceptions in the law regarding people involved in religion, such as priests and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tihic. [In English] I have another document, and this is the code of All People's Defence, and I would ask the usher to help me with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we leave the document, the excerpt from the constitution, we haven't got the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't got it still, but we are trying hard to get the full translation of all the relevant laws, codes and constitutions, and we will definitely provide the Trial Chamber as soon as we get all these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Provided you don't forget to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what year was this constitution passed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Basically, this is the constitution of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia issued in 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Any amendments thereafter to these particular articles you read? Have they been in force since 1974?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Just on this issue of translation -- now, in this particular case, I don't think there will be any problems, because I don't think I'm going to re-examine on this issue. I can't say, because I haven't heard all of the evidence, but thus far, it doesn't look likely to me that I'll be re-examining on this. But the question might arise in future with the documents, where, if a document is produced, and I've got no translation, I'm handicapped, I can't possibly re-examine on a document if I don't know what it says. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not causing a problem today, and I'm not objecting or anything like that, but as I sit here, I was thinking to myself, if I had wanted to, I wouldn't have been able to ask a single question about these documents because I can't read them. You can see the sort of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I've said this before, I think even in the Status Conference before the trial actually started. I did say that Defence counsel should provide the documents they are going to use in cross-examination to the Prosecution beforehand so that they can look at them, they can see what they can do with them. And if you can't get the English translation, even in that case, you still give the Serbo-Croat copies to the Prosecution, because they may try and get their own draft translation for purposes of being able to re-examine the witness. This is important, because even if it's in Serbo-Croat, at least it will be of some help to the Prosecution to know that there is a document which is going to be used in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I might just mention to you that I did remember seeing a copy of a book called "The Constitutions of the World." I think it's published in America, and I do not know whether this particular constitution is there or not, but you just might want to look up the library in Belgrade or somewhere, and you might just get the whole constitution there in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for instructing me, Your Honour. This is the constitution that is not in force. So I will do my best to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D12/4 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, before we go on to discuss this document that -- or, rather, the Law on Total National Defence or All People's Defence, I should like to get a brief explanation from you. The constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was in keeping with the federal constitution, was it not? It could not regulate certain issues in a different manner, could it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell me, the document that you have before you, is it the Law on Total National Defence or All People's Defence -- or part of that law, to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, the Law on Total National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for the poor copy of the document, so please, if you find it difficult to read something out that I'm going to ask you to read, please tell me and I shall read it out for you, and you will say whether you agree or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel, what was the date when this one was passed? And is it still in force?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It is from April 23, 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it still in force?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. We are talking about Bosnia, and definitely it is not in power in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. When did it fall out? When did it stop being applicable?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, by forming a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It was in force during the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When the SFRY existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm referring to that period, in 1990 and 1991 and beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because this is another problem. You have indicated that you are calling a constitutional law expert. Why don't we leave these applicable laws and what have you to that expert? Because this is a fact witness. I know that he's a lawyer, but he's not here as a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have this in mind. What is the issue of this? I am trying to build a base for some information that this witness gave us through his testimony in regard to Yugoslav People's Army, its relation to Territorial Defence, and for this reason I'm just using portions of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because there is a danger in precisely using the portions, because it's very easy to read a portion out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can assure the Court that the full documents will be tendered to the Court, so the Prosecution and the Court will have these complete documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So that if this witness makes a mistake in legal interpretation of the effect of this legislation, you can't hold him to that, because he's not an expert. Because these are the dangers of mixing, you know, fact witnesses with expert witnesses, the way you handle the two. You understand what I'm saying? So I do hope that the way you use this legislation will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. If you would just bear, just for one minute, with me, I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- conflict with the division of classification of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will try, then, to do it in some easier way for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'm sorry, but perhaps you may want to enlighten us on what this witness' understanding is as to Territorial Defence in respect of the whole Republic of Yugoslavia then, Bosnia-Herzegovina specifically, and the area around Bosanski Samac. What is his understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, you heard the guidance of the Trial Chamber, and so I'm going to ask you some questions along those lines and in that way. I'm interested in some of the articles of this law which bear upon the formation of the Territorial Defence, the position of the Yugoslav People's Army, the relationship between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, so something in that realm. Now, I just want to ask you: Does the law on All Peoples Defence in the course of 1991 and, let us say, up until the proclamation of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its recognition, was it applied and in force on the Territorial Defence of BH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was it applied to the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality, by that same token?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, in Bosanski Samac too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now perhaps look through some articles, a small number, although I had planned to ask you some more questions in that area. Could we first take a look at Article 95, point 1, para 1. I'm going to ask you for your opinion. I am fully conscious of the fact that you are not an expert on constitutional law, but in view of the fact that you are a legal man yourself and a politician, a lawyer, perhaps we can deduce something and reach some conclusions as to what was written in the laws of the day and their provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May we agree that on the basis of that particular article, Article 95, if it says so in that law, "Organisation, preparation, and leadership of the Territorial Defence in the republics and autonomous provinces is carried out by the competent organs in the republics and autonomous provinces, in keeping with the constitution and the law"? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now just a brief question with respect to the following article, Article 96. Would you take a look at that article, please. Does it state in Article 96 that the armed forces are commanded by organs of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please turn the page to Article 97, where it states, in the first paragraph, the following -- would you read it out, actually?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Article 97. By decision of the Presidency of the SFRY, for certain areas, unified commands may be established for units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army and Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. This legal provision, as I understand it, allows for the possibility of forming, establishing, for certain given regions, a united, unique command of the Yugoslav People's Army and the TO. Am I right? Do you understand it in that way too?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these laws, and the constitution, resolve questions when you are faced with a foreign enemy, when Yugoslavia is being attacked by an outside enemy and not an internal one, not the settlement of internal political questions. It refers to attack from outside, when Yugoslavia is attacked from a foreign enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think I got what you're saying. Oh, you're talking about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have our break and resume at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination is continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, before you begin, I just thought that I could be of some assistance to you. During the coffee break, I laid my hands, for obvious reasons, on an English version of the 1974 constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in its entirety, which is in the library here at the ICTY. And maybe that might save the expense of translation. It was published in Belgrade in 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the Prosecution can also get it right away. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honour for having assisted us in that way. We will make -- we will get ourselves a permanent copy and keep it here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Especially in case you wanted to raise anything with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I might just add that the other constitutions, I think before and after 1992, are all on the Internet. You can access them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, may we proceed? Let me just ask you then, without looking into this document further, does it say here that it is the presidency of the SFRY that orders mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war, in case of immediate threat of war, and other extraordinary circumstances, mobilisation of the armed forces is ordered by the presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that is what I underlined; is that right? Now I would like to ask you to look at the last page of that document. That is the Official Gazette of the SFRY, page 594, Friday, the 17th of May. Now I would like to ask you to look at the right-hand column, the first paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commanders of the Territorial Defence of municipalities and other socio-political communities in the republic, i.e., autonomous province, shall be appointed by the commander of the Territorial Defence of the republic, i.e., autonomous province. Paragraph 2 becomes -- hitherto paragraph 2 becomes paragraph 3."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question because it overlapped the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, you are overlapping the answers of the witness so they didn't hear what you said after the witness completed his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
