utterances.text: And is it the same one with the 31st of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And 31st October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would rather have it complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just waited for translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 20 of that statement, in the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And to help my learned friend from the Prosecution, English version without ERN number but the page is 20, on the same statement, English version, so they can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, on page 20 of your statement, paragraph 2, you stated the following to the Prosecutor: "While I was in Batajnica, I learnt that Izet Izetbegovic, Alija Fitozovic, Omer Nalic, Safet Hadzialijagic, and I had all been sentenced to death. This decision was announced by Vecernje Novosti and was supposedly signed by Irfan Ajanovic. I knew the news was untrue, but it was disturbing." You remember having said that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that you did not state those details when the Prosecutor asked you, may we now agree that that was what the situation was actually like, that that was what happened?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to another point, another detail: On page 16 of the statement we're discussing, that is to say the 1994 statement -- [In English] English version is also without ERN number, but it's page 16, and the other part is page 17, English version. [Interpretation] In your statement to the Prosecutor, you state the following: "When we got onto the helicopter, which was a military helicopter, there was a coffin inside, and there was somebody in the coffin with a Serbian name, aged 20. Later I heard that 'Lugar' killed 20 people, because this person had been killed. I think that his name was 'Vuk.' Izet Izetbegovic knows the family he comes from. The family name could have been Vukmirovic." You remember making that statement, do you not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There was probably a mix-up. I don't know it is an essential point, but you answered, in response to the Prosecutor, on page 1482, line 7 and 8, that the name of the person who had been killed and the name on the coffin was Vuk Mirovic, Vuk being the first name and Mirovic being the last name. So let's clarify that point. I mean, we've -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the surname was Vukmirovic, one word, just the last name, Vukmirovic. So it wasn't a name plus a surname. Whether it was Vukmirovic, Vuksanovic, or some other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. They were just details from the transcript. Mr. Tihic, you are an experienced lawyer. You were a judge, you were a prosecutor, and an attorney; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On this day, how much working experience, professional experience, do you have as of today, looking back?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from July 1974 I've been working, which would make it - let me see - 27 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, 27 years. Thank you. I assume that you graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From the statement that you gave on the 28th of February, 1995 to the OTP, I see that you were the legal advisor, counsellor, of the embassy of BH. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What embassy was that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the legal advisor, councillor, of the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Bonn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Germany, you mean?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are the vice-president of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After you were released from detention, I think that I read somewhere that you also were deputy minister for foreign affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or some such post.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. No, nothing like it. Nothing similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you were in the foreign affairs ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And which post did you hold? What was your position there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the head of the department for consular affairs. That is the lowest level of the leadership cadres of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after that post, you went to Bonn to be a legal advisor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was vice-president of the party in 1999 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was a professional post with a tenure?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sure that during your student days, during your studies, you studied a subject called international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Public law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Public law, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the course of your professional activities in foreign affairs, you also had contact with legal affairs of the international type, with an international character?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, connected to consular affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, as far as I know, you became the president of the Municipal Board of the SDA in Samac sometime in 1991, and before that the president was Izet Izetbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that you had some other function within the SDA party at the BH level, or was that the only function you had?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Main Board as well of the Party of Democratic Action. That is a body made up of 120 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell me when you were elected member of the Main Board of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the first congress, November 1991. I think it was November, at least. Yes, November 1991. It could have been October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You became president of the Municipal Board of the SDA and were then elected to the Main Board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the first congress that was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And since 1991, you have been a member of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was re-elected at the second congress as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Up until the latest elections, when you became party president; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, Mr. Izetbegovic, can you agree with me that in the period before the elections in BH in 1990, that there was a general atmosphere prevailing in political circles that the communist power and authority ought to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume you'll agree with me when I say that the SDA party, the HDZ and SDS parties had a sort of unofficial or official relationships in the sense of jointly appearing with the aim of pooling their efforts and appearing jointly with the aim of toppling communist rule; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards that end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that period of time - and the Prosecutor asked you about the character and nature of the parties, and I don't think that was sufficiently explained - you will agree with me when I say that those three parties were national parties and not nationalistic parties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the election results of 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS formed their own rule, got the vote, because they won and they formed the government?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the top level, not the local level. I'm talking about the republican government.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, an inter-party arrangement was being bandied about, a system by which -- a system which was called "five-four-three" -- which was referred to as the "five-four-three" system or principle?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out here. As far as I understand it, it was an inter-party arrangement between the SDA, SDZ and SDS that that would be the ratio and division of power - I'm thinking about the posts, the ministerial posts - and that that would be in the ratio of five, four, three. If you don't remember, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly it was that way but I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one by one. You will agree, I think, that to all practical purposes, the basis of the FRY -- SFRY, was a meeting in 1943 in Jajce, when the future state was formed with constituent people, constitutive peoples and so on and so forth; that was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 29th of November, 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And throughout the existence of this former Yugoslavia, there was a principle of national tolerance, a balance that was struck? I mean it in that sense. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that was particularly present in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where it was consistently implemented fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right. Because of the three peoples, three religions, a multitude of various interrelationships; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The communist rule, the communist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, really strove against any kind of national reactions from any of the three sides, and they actually tried people for that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This system of respecting the interests of all three peoples in Bosnia in 1990, when the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS had a common political objective, was also observed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the highest positions were being filled, that was also observed. However, it was the vote, the outcome of the vote, that was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will agree that we were talking about proportionality. Those who got the largest vote got the largest number of positions, and proportionally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who got the largest number of votes had the right to choose the top position, and then the second-largest party would have the right to get the second-most-important position, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us just help the interpreters. We speak the same language. When I finish my question, perhaps you could wait for it to be interpreted and then you answer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do tend to speed a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also, you are very experienced. You have testified in quite a few cases here in The Hague, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, not really, only in this case and in one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back to Samac. The SDA in Samac won two seats in the municipal parliament; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Some other parties won more seats than the SDA in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, following a political agreement reached at a higher level between the SDA, the HDZ and SDS at the municipal level in Bosanski Samac, a coalition was set up between the HDZ, the SDS and the SDA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether it was a coalition or whatever, it simply -- as you say, this was a principle that was followed from the top downwards, because for a coalition you need to have an agreement in writing, what would be done, how it would be done, by what ways and means, et cetera. However, some kind of alliance, informal alliance, which was hard to obtain. Actually, we could agree on all other issues with the exception of the future of Yugoslavia, or rather Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for these vital issues, I don't think that there were really any problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. So call it what we will. Let it be a political alliance, an alliance that is in government at local level.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that before it is established in this way, that all of you communicated between and among yourselves and sought ways and means of establishing some kind of alliance. I'm referring to the parties at local level.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an alliance and agreement while we were choosing people for these positions, and after that, things started going wrong all over. Because there was this question of the future of Yugoslavia and Bosnia that cropped up, and that was a source of tensions, conflicts, and people stopped doing what they were elected to do, and that is to resolve municipal problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We will agree that that's the way things go in politics. There are difficulties on some days. That's politics. Anything is possible in politics, isn't it? All kinds of alliances?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there is a wise proverb that says it's better to have a good divorce than a bad marriage; isn't that right? Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you heard of yet another saying: Birds of a feather flock together? Have you heard of that one?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can agree that towards the end of October 1991 there was quite a bit of tension and difficulty in parliamentary life in Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, you certainly know that, because I think that by then you had already become a member of the Main Board; isn't that right? You said sometime in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were endless parliamentary debates that went on until dawn; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm suffering from an inability to see where this is going, and there's been quite a bit of this, and I had hoped that the relevance of it would become apparent. It's rapidly, I think, becoming a discussion of political history. Now, unless it can somehow be linked to the indictment or the issues that concern Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Pantelic, then of course it's not particularly relevant. But I've racked my brains to try and think of how it could possibly be linked to an issue in the indictment, and I simply can't come up with anything. Now, it's got to the point where I suggest that Mr. Pantelic should outline to the Chamber and say, "Well, look, this is the relevance of this material. This is what I'm hoping to elicit or achieve" or "This is my objective," and then perhaps my objective will be ill-founded. But at this stage I'm troubled by the fact -- the apparent lack of relevance, and I don't think my objection is premature, given the length of time that we've been on this topic, on these sorts of topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps counsel can explain the relevance of the line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President, gladly. My aim is to defend my client. That's my first thing. And also, due to the fact that this indictment covers also a period in 1995 [sic], including various forms, such as planning, instigating, ordering, et cetera, et cetera, I would be very happy if my learned friend will drop the charges against my client until the 17th of April, 1992, and then I will not pose the questions. Otherwise, I think that I'm entitled to go into the relevance of the political life from the, let's say, republican level up to the local level, to see the connections, to see maybe - who knows? - personal role or involvement of this witness in all these events. Because it's from 1991. So yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just a clarification. I see, and I think I also heard, you say the indictment covers also a period in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. 1991, I said. Sorry. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I heard, and it also came out on the words, as 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My mistake maybe. It's 1991, preparation of all these events, and then until the end of -- maybe that was my -- I do apologise, Your Honour. So in short, that's my intention: to see what is the situation on that level, how the governmental functions was established, and then to see how it was worked on the local level, simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can -- yes. I think that's understandable, since there is the issue of statehood here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the subject matter. And also, let me add, Madam President, that this particular witness, Mr. Tihic, is not only a fact witness; he is, according to the list provided from the Prosecution to Defence, is also a so-called contextual witness about all these events. So that's the aim of my questioning. So he's not speaking about the isolated event in time framework and place, et cetera. Thank you so much. I will proceed, with your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- with your permission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, sometime towards the end of October 1991, in the republican parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a decision was passed on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either in October or some other month, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We will agree that during this decision-making in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb MPs left that session.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't agree fully, because part of the MPs of other parties were Serbs, from the SDP, from the Reformist forces, et cetera, and they did not leave the session. However, the SDS [Realtime transcript read in error "SDA"] MPs did leave the session. So the larger part of Serb MPs did leave the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also the MPs of the SPO, which is also a Serb party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, no objection, but I just wonder if there's a mistake in the transcript, line -- page 100, just a few lines ago, at line 11, says: "The SDA MPs did leave the session." Is that what the witness said, or did he say SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: SDS. SDS. MR. DI FAZIO: That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He said SDS. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the question maybe for clarification, if it's necessary, I mean this particular part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Just so that we know which party it was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. [Interpretation] There was a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please say that the SDS MPs left parliament? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me, as an experienced lawyer and politician, that the question of sovereignty is a capital question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could say that this question affects the vital interests of all the three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the declaration speaks of sovereignty of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you. I wasn't speaking about the declaration, and I have another question now. But please, when the Prosecutor re-examines you, then you will be able to explain that. You see, we have a principle here. When the Defence cross-examines, that is rather narrow.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We will agree, Mr. Tihic, that in the constitutional system of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and in 1991, and of course earlier as well, the principle of the protection of interests of all three constituent peoples was present and built into the constitution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We will agree that sometime during 1991 - I think that this was twice, one in February and one in June - that amendments were adopted to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right? If you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that some chambers were abolished, and the name "socialist" was dropped. It was only "republic." I can't remember sufficiently. There were some minor changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It depends on your point of view. Within these changes, there was a separate chamber of nationalities that was envisaged that would take care of the balance of the rights of all three nationalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wasn't that a commission? There was a commission for the protection of vital national interests. I think that is what it was. And the chamber of nationalities was at state level, wasn't it, of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Whatever. You do have some recollections of that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness is talking about a commission and not a chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is hard now to go into the merit of this issue, because we shall wait for the expert witnesses with the real wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- amendments, et cetera. I mean, I will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Press.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- to press and to go into the area where neither witness nor me would be -- just in general that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He may not remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, because he just gave me that answer, so I don't want to push anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably recall that after the Serb MPs left the republican parliament, on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991, a plebiscite of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina was held. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, can I have a second? I have a lot of papers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes. Thank you. I found the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this plebiscite on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991 - and the subject was the establishment of some Serb entity, or whatever we would call it, within Bosnia-Herzegovina - you are probably aware of the fact that on the 9th of January, 1992, actually, the Republika Srpska was proclaimed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you are the vice-president of the parliament of Republika Srpska, you may know that the constitution of the Republika Srpska was adopted on the 28th of February, 1992, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But nowadays, because you are vice-president of the national assembly of Republika Srpska, we will agree that the Republika Srpska functions from a legal point of view on the basis of its constitution that was adopted in 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree on that. Republika Srpska functions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me, I know -- MR. DI FAZIO: The witness should be permitted to finish his answer, surely, particularly as it's in answer to a question asked by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To allow him to explain? MR. DI FAZIO: The question was: "Because you're vice-president, you agree that the Republika Srpska functions from a legal point of view on the basis of its constitution that was adopted; isn't that right?" The witness says, "No, we can't," and starts to explain why, and is cut off. Now, surely, he must be permitted to give his answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, but let me phrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Tihic, the present-day Republika Srpska functions on the basis of the constitution that was adopted in 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The present-day Republika Srpska, does it function on the basis of some other constitution? Please explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska functions on the basis of the Dayton Agreement, Annex 4 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the legal basis, and since then there has been this entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina that has been recognised and that is called Republika Srpska. The previous constitutions, at least the first one, was annulled by the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the one from February, the one that you refer to, February, 1992. Because the only thing that does have legitimacy is the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, as such, was admitted into the United Nations, which in 1995, on the basis of the Dayton Agreement, became the legal adherent, Bosnia-Herzegovina consisting of two entities, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, that is. Since then, Republika Srpska has been in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your answer, you raised a few subjects and now we have to clarify them a bit. Are you aware of a doctrine in international public law de facto state and de jure state? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if I could ask you for a little clarification on this, it's my understanding of public international law that the distinction between de jure and de facto is reserved for the governments of states, not the states themselves per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, you Honour. I will rephrase my question on that line. In fact, I was referring to the issue of recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But let's put this question. It might be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Honourable Judge Williams has made a certain proposal and could you please tell me whether you are perhaps familiar with the theory of de facto and de jure governments in international law? Do you know about that subject matter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is the same. Yes, but not sufficiently in order for me to be able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Izetbegovic -- I beg your pardon, I beg your pardon. Mr. Tihic, I beg your pardon, in Article 1 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Annex 4 to the Dayton Agreement, paragraph 3 reads that Bosnia-Herzegovina shall consist of two entities, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska. We agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible answer]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since yesterday, I think during the cross-examination, you mentioned the option that it is impossible to have a state that would be called the Republic of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct? You said something like that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the Official Gazette cannot be called "The Official Gazette of the Serb People." You see, an official gazette can be an official gazette of an entity, of a canton, of a state, not of a people. People do not publish official gazettes. Socio-political communities, states, issue, publish, official gazettes, and it says over there, "The Official Gazette of the Serb People." That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Tihic, you probably did not notice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You Honour, the witness did answer the previous question but very softly and it's not there, line -- there is no answer after that, and perhaps the question can be repeated, because there was no audible answer to that question. And we need it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you Honour. There is a problem in the transcript. I will ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, we spoke here about Article 1 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Annex 1 [as interpreted] to the Dayton Agreement, paragraph 3, and there are two entities, and do we agree on that? And your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you didn't notice yesterday in the Official Gazette it says, "In BH," in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Madam President, I have with me one copy, so maybe I can give it to the witness and then he can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, he's, well, trying to charge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to know the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's "The Official Gazette of Serbian People in B and H." He said no, it cannot be Official Gazette only of Serbian people. It should be some kind of state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We haven't had that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was admitted with ID numbers yesterday. Various decisions and orders of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can search for it. What was the ID, the number, for identification purposes only?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You Honour, there were seven of these documents admitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have one of them, you Honour, so if it's -- I will not tender that into exhibits, just if you will allow me to given it to Mr. Tihic to read this title, and then he will give the answer after that, if it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He can go ahead and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's rather linguistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We just want to make sure the record is correct as to which document is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We refer to documents by -- we identify documents by their numbers. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think the number is rather important given the fact that I don't have a translation. I've got absolutely no idea what's in these documents, and the issue that I raised earlier this morning, of course, I'm not going to seek to stop it on this occasion, but the difficulty the Prosecution labours under in these circumstances is apparent, and I'll just make that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's wait for the document list to be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: These were the Official Gazettes tendered by Mr. Zecevic during his cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Milan Simic, various decrees, government decisions, et cetera, et cetera, which were published in Official Gazette of Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I remembered that Mr. Tihic read it very, very -- in detailed form. So you can get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can't find it, Your Honour. There were nine documents and they were all in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the usher collect those nine documents and then show them to counsel? And then counsel should use -- should call them by their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, now, I would like to present to Mr. Tihic the D12/2 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to read the heading of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, just read the portion where we have the number of the Official Gazette: what it is, who it is, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Monday, the 8th of June, 1992, Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 8, page 317."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's all with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Usher, it's okay. You can collect all the documents. It was just for this proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Republika Srpska, as it was formed, had different titles and names. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that's quite a normal thing in the development of a state or subject, to change names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do we need another microphone to be switched on for the interpreters, or one is okay? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it has to be switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From your experience as a legal man and politician, could you tell us what attributes a state needs to have to be called a state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I don't think the question is for this witness, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw. I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will agree with me, Mr. Tihic, when I say that a state, amongst other attributes, must have a central government? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are going back through the back door. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic. MR. DI FAZIO: It's very much the back door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Perhaps if I may seek a clarification from you, Mr. Tihic. You said it wasn't a state. You see, after the plebiscite in 1991, plebiscite of the Serb people, you had the Republic of Srpska -- the Republic of Srpska from January 1992. Now, you said that that wasn't a state. Can you give us your reasons why you say that that was not a state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, because the plebiscite was not a legal one. The decision about a plebiscite was not brought by the competent authorities, on the basis of the constitutional authorities that were authorised to take a decision of that kind, so the existing legal system in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not respected. Next, the referendum that was held on the basis of this unconstitutional plebiscite, which was also not recognised, either in Bosnia-Herzegovina or outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the relevant international factors. A society gets together, says, "We're a state." That's not enough. There must be recognition. It must be within the legal system, with a legal basis and foundation, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and somebody must recognise it as being legal. Who controlled the plebiscite and referendum? How many people went out to vote? On the basis of what lists? Everything was done outside all this framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Did the Muslims and the Croats participate in this plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, neither the Muslims nor the Croats took part, and quite a number of Serbs didn't take part either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And to follow on from what you were saying, do you know that 1,350,000 citizens of Serb ethnicity took part in the plebiscite? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is propaganda. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't that many Serbs in Bosnia at all, so how could they take part in the voting, that many?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, once again, could you just limit yourself to answering my questions. We don't want to make a political forum here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the questions are of that nature that it warrants it sometimes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May we agree that the present Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the basis of the constitution from the Dayton Agreement, has joint functions in foreign policy, does it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Foreign trade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Customs and tariffs policies?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Monetary policy?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And among other things, international cooperation, international obligations, legal, et cetera, the control of air traffic, and so on and so forth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the moment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are two armies, are there not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One is in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the other one is in Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the moment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have an existence of two types or two groups of police forces. One group is in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you can divide them into types.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, one police force.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a police force in the Federation and in Republika Srpska. They are the same police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But they don't have a joint command, do they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they work similarly. They have similar rules and regulations governing their activity, they cooperate, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is it composed of cantons, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ten cantons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All these cantons have their own assemblies and constitutions, don't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska has a national assembly, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It has its own government; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And only a limited portion of competences of those two entities which we have enumerated have been transferred to the main organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They haven't been transferred. They are the source of this parent authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Even though I'm very interested in statehood and public international law, I'm just wondering whether you could clarify me whether, pursuant to our Rules on cross-examination, where this line of questioning is falling. Is it limited to the -- in some way to the subject matter of the evidence in chief or to matters affecting the credibility of the witness? I find it very interesting, but I'm just wondering where we're going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, absolutely. This line of questioning doesn't have any relation to the credibility of this witness, absolutely not. This is a subject matter, I want to clarify with this witness, the development of Republika Srpska in 1991, 1992, with regards to the final form which is practically recognised by the Dayton Peace Accord in 1995. So that was the line. So I can maybe go to the narrow matter now. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, because I was just wondering how -- say again, how it ties in to the time period, time periods, with respect to the alleged crimes contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. The situation is very simple. We have a process of development of one entity, no matter whether it is the state or entity or maybe autonomous province from time A until time B, and a part of this development is the subject matter of this case, 1999 -- 1991, sorry, and until the end of 1993. So I'm trying to establish a, I would say, development and parallel view of these two points, in fact. And with this line of questioning about the existence of Republika Srpska within the framework of the Dayton Peace Accord, I'm done, I'm finished. So now I'm focusing to the period of 1991 and 1992 with regard to the political activities where obviously this witness and the other persons were involved. Thank you. [Interpretation] Would you just please put your second microphone on, Mr. Tihic. MR. DI FAZIO: There's a couple of matters that arise. I'm going to ask my learned colleague to address you very briefly on something arising from the agreed facts, because I think she's better versed on that, and I believe it's relevant to this issue that was raised by Your Honour Judge Williams. But if we may go back to the Rule, Rule 90(H)(2), cross-examination of the witness arises under three headings: credibility, which is not -- doesn't give rise to this line of cross-examination. The second two limbs on which you can launch upon a cross-examination are clear. If it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: -- the subject matter of the evidence in chief -- and I don't recall this witness talking about these issues at all in his evidence in chief. So therefore, we go back to the very last limb, and that's what Mr. Pantelic, in his submission to Judge Williams' question, did not answer, and that is evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. Now, he hasn't explained, with respect to Mr. Pantelic, how this evidence is relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. And, of course, and of course, don't let's forget, don't let's forget, that we don't know what the case is, because none of their cases -- none of these defendants are putting their cases to the witness, and they're not putting it to Mr. Tihic. So we don't know -- we've got no way of -- the best you can do is gaze into a crystal ball and think, well -- speculate as to what the defence might be. So they're not complying with (H)(2), and it becomes very difficult then to justify cross-examination under (H)(1) when you don't know what the case is. Now, Mr. Pantelic should, with respect, make it very clear how this evidence relates directly to a defence that he is going to raise, because we know that's the last limb under which he can get this sort of questioning in, and it's not been explained, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because I think the problem is that the counsel is dealing with the present-day situation as opposed to the period covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's one of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just tried to explain. But let me add a very short explanation. If Mr. Tihic will be a witness in cross-examination answering very simply yes or no, we would not have this kind of problem. Because if in the record, in transcript, we have all his expanded answers, I'm obliged to ask him on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if he makes some references, you know, with regard to the 1991, 1992, existence of Republika Srpska, so forth and so on, I am obliged to have another line of questioning. So I kindly ask Mr. Tihic to give me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's the time period --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- which is covered by your questions. That is where the problem is. It is present-day -- the present-day situation and not the situation between 1991 and December 1993, because that is the period covered by the indictment. And we are simply saying we would like the questions in cross-examination to cover that period and also to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I concur, Your Honour. I will proceed. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, in 1992, Republika Srpska had its government, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, in 1992, after January 1992, of course, had its own presidency, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, in 1992, had its own army, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Explain, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, there was the Yugoslav People's Army. It wasn't the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May we agree with the fact that Republika Srpska at that time had its own police force, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we agree with the fact that the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska was Ratko Mladic, General Ratko Mladic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The commanders changed. I don't know whether Mladic was commander in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness said the Republika Srpska didn't have its own army. It was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is what I was trying to establish, Your Honour, because with this particular question, I mean, I just put to the witness a question who was the -- and he said right, that was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we are not waiting for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't want to interrupt. Was Your Honour about to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted the witness to explain, if there was an army in Republika Srpska, if there was, under whose control was that army? What was -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's this very issue that I wanted to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To clarify with the witness? MR. DI FAZIO: And with the Chamber and with Mr. Pantelic, because as my colleague, Ms. Reidy, rightly points out, there were agreed facts in this case, by way of motion, that were put in some -- quite some time ago, I can't recall exactly, I don't have them to hand. However, it was an agreed fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a state after a certain point, 22nd of May of 1992, and we are not, at least by that point, at least by that point. Now, these questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're saying it was an agreed fact between the parties. Can you just repeat that, that Bosnia and Herzegovina -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will. Will Your Honour just give me a moment to confer with my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour, it is absolutely not the situation. We have an official notice of admission of Bosnia and Herzegovina into the UN on 22nd of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's hear Mr. di Fazio and you will be given an opportunity to respond. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to hand the floor from the Prosecution to my colleague Ms. Reidy, who is better acquainted with the material, and she can explain more clearly than I can, so I'll ask her to address the Chamber on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The point that the Prosecution would like to make is that it's not -- wasn't in the joint statement of agreed facts, but directly in response to a motion by Mr. Pantelic on behalf of his client, it was agreed that on the 22nd of May, Bosnia-Herzegovina, would become -- would at least, at the very latest then, was admitted on the 22nd of May, 1992, as a member of the United Nations, and that his debate, dispute, is before that. He's arguing that it may or may not have been a state. But it's clear in the motion that it was conceded that that is the last cut-off date in which they are willing to argue that Bosnia-Herzegovina may not have been a state. So I think that when -- what flows from that is that when Mr. Pantelic is putting questions, whether it's to do with an army or a police force pertaining to Republika Srpska, he is very clear in which period he's talking about, January 1992, prior to 19th of May, 1992, prior to the 6th of March, 1992, because we are all very well aware that there are significant dates in 1992 when there is dispute as to the status which entities have reached. Whether in fact it was all or part of the JNA, but just given a name as a cover, which as you know has been the Prosecution case throughout many, many cases in this Tribunal. So I think it is misleading for the transcript, and also perhaps misleading to the witness, if Mr. Pantelic is not very specific as to the time frame in 1992 he talks about, as I said, takes on board the fact that we have already accepted that the 22nd of May is a cut-off date for his argument about statehood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was also my intention when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hope the translation has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Has it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the -- my idea was to ask the witness about the existence of the Army of Republika Srpska throughout the period -- all the period, and he said no. After that, I was obliged to go to another line to put him another question, and I was very keen to allow him to explain us whether maybe he's thinking that JNA was from 1992 to 1995 official army, or maybe it's some other army, so I was very, as I said, keen to allow him to give us the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. While some conclusions cannot be made by this witness, some facts as to actually what was happening or what was in existence then can be asked of the witness, but please do clear up the period which you are talking about. You heard Ms. Reidy talking about the fact that it was admitted to the UN on 22nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So if the witness can be directed to which period your questions are stemming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, you have heard what we have been saying. We are discussing 1992. That's what we are talking about now. Would you please give us your view about Republika Srpska. Was there an army there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was it before May or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of January to the 31st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the 1st of January, to the 31st of December; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least for the first six months, the JNA was actually in Bosnia-Herzegovina officially and in actual fact. After that, after that, parts of the JNA stayed on in Bosnia-Herzegovina but they put on different uniforms. They were the uniforms of the Army of Republika Srpska, as it was called, but the command was still in Belgrade, and throughout the war it was from the General Staff of the Yugoslav army in Belgrade that the influence was wielded on military operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was also financed from there, logistic support, and in all other senses, cadres and so on and so forth, and it was only the other day that some of the last vestiges were cleared up from the war that was financed in Belgrade. So there was a portion of the Yugoslav People's Army there throughout the war in actual fact. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you. That's your opinion as a layman. You are not a military expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, as far as I am able to follow politics, but no, I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, do you know the JNA was demobilised sometime in May or June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, all its equipment and materiel, storehouses, airports, helicopters, tanks, planes, it just changed the emblems. It no longer said "JNA." It said "Army of Republika Srpska." But everything else, financing, logistics, command, remained the same. Everything was directed from Belgrade. Of course, a portion was independent, that is to say the commanders of the Republika Srpska and the army grew stronger, but Belgrade retained its influence, the influence it wielded, and took part in the operations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break or maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So the arms stayed there, but the personnel stayed there, the army personnel stayed there, but the uniforms were changed? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They changed the emblems and insignia on their uniforms. The uniforms stayed the same. They just changed the patches and emblems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And did this new uniform army have a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. It was called the Army of the Republika Srpska or something like that. I'm not sure what Republika Srpska's name was at the time so it changed its name analogously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will have a short break and continue at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. --- Break taken at 4.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue with cross-examination, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, may we agree with the assertation that at the end of October, when the Serb deputies left the BH parliament, that in fact Bosnia-Herzegovina ceased to function and exist; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May we agree, Mr. Tihic, that in the period between November to January, from November 1991 to January 1992, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that communities of the Croatian people were Herceg-Bosna, Central Bosnia, and Bosanska Posavina, that those three communities were formed; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those communities did exist, but I don't know whether that was the period. I'm not sure of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we agree with the fact that the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the period after the 6th of April, 1992, was not in a position to control -- was not capable of controlling the overall territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What does the answer mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You believe that it was in a position to control it; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh. No.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it could not control the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I said. Because the Yugoslav People's Army did not allow them to do so as well as various paramilitary formations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please be so kind as to answer the following question: Which is the territory that the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled in the period after the 6th of April, 1992? If you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This territory changed. I mean, it certainly controlled Sarajevo, Zenica, or rather, the area of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have the assistance of Mr. Usher. Maybe we could have the Times map here. It would be easier maybe to follow these explanations, because some of us may not be so familiar with the regions. With your permission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can have the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't know what is the exhibit number, but obviously the map is there. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the number of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is Prosecution Exhibit P15.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please get up, Mr. Tihic, take off your headphones and take the other headphones with the microphone and use the pointer, please? It's going to be easier for you because this pointer is short. Please, could you move from one region to the other, one district to the other? [In English] Do you hear me? Do you copy me? Ten-4. Thank you. [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness. There is usually another microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, there is another microphone with a cord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The one which is hand-held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, so-called show microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tihic, let's go back to the beginning of your answer. Please show us on this map which regions were held by the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the time after the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The size of the territory varied. First of all, Sarajevo, as a city. Then here, from Visoko, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Approximately when? Could you give us approximately the timing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visoko, Zenica, Travnik, you see. Central Bosnia was always under its control. Tuzla and the Tuzla area was always under their control as well. Bihac and this area too also, always. Then down here Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, Eastern Mostar, that was also constantly under their control. And now a certain towns changed, like Srebrenica and Zepa here. And then Gorazde was also under the control of the central government, over here in eastern Bosnia, things like that. Then this part of Herzegovina, Herzegovina. It depended on whether it was before or after the Washington Accords, the situation varied. So it's Bihac, central Bosnia, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Mostar over here, Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Let the record show that the witness explained on the Exhibit P15 the regions under the control of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period of from mid-April 1992 and the other areas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you referred to all these areas. Could you please tell us approximately what is the percentage of territory that the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled then, as against not in its control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the way it was. As for territory itself, the central government controlled -- actually, it depended on whether it was at war with Herceg-Bosna or not. So from 30 to 40 per cent, but as far as the population is concerned, the number was much larger because the largest centres, after all, were under the control of the central government, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, Mostar. So it must have been over 50 per cent of the population. But then, as far as territory is concerned, it was between 30 and 40 per cent, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you please get the other microphone closer and turn it on, the one that's the same like the one you're facing here, and please turn it on so the interpreters could hear you? Thank you. Bearing in mind what you've just said, Mr. Tihic, you will certainly agree with me when I read the words of an Australian professor of international law, Professor Roland Rich in connection with the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In an essay of his, he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to Mr. Pantelic asking questions about factual matters, control of the area, things that Mr. Tihic might have known about. Mr. Tihic was asked about his knowledge of international law, and I think he made quite clear that while he worked in a consulate, he is not an expert of international law. I don't think this is an appropriate question to ask about an international law expert. Whether or not Professor Rich is an expert or not is something that Mr. Pantelic is of course well able to put on the record when he calls his own expert. The factual problem is not the problem. It's for Mr. Pantelic to use those facts within the confines of his legal argument on the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I do think that this question is beyond the scope of Mr. Tihic. He is a lawyer but not an international lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's an essay of the professor so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, Madam President, this is the factual issue, not legal, and not theoretical. This is exactly the factual issue. If you allow me to read it to the witness and then you can see whether if has any relevance or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, because you're asking the witness to comment, and that's an international law essay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is not international law, Madam President. It's a factual issue about the territory, as I said. Probably you will agree with me because, as you said, with regard to the territory that it was not the case that the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I will not allow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just in support of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, you can use it, as Ms. Reidy said, to bolster your argument, but not put it to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: -- I have one more question to ask you. The Tadic case, on appeal, hasn't it decided all these issues, I mean, about the JNA forces, demobilising, territory under control of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government and issues of that nature which you are raising now? Is there any evidence that you're presenting questions in cross-examination which will take us beyond that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Tadic case, and the judgement in Tadic case, was rendered in the circumstances where Defence were not in situation to present all proofs, and from my modest point of view as a small lawyer, you know, international terms, I think that it's a miscarriage of justice regarding to factual things, and we in this case are trying to expand and to go beyond this. Finally, this Trial Chamber [indiscernible]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, you know Muhamed Filipovic, or at least by name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He is a well-respected businessman and theoretician, and an intellectual, indeed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not a businessman. That least of all. He's an academician, a professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We can agree that Mr. Muhamed Filipovic was one of the important founders of the SDA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was a founder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But he was in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We can also agree that Mr. Muhamed Filipovic was persecuted by the Communist authorities after the Second World War and he had to emigrate?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have confused him with Zulfikarpasic. No. No. Muhamed was never persecuted, never. You are referring to Adil Begzulfikarpasic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, Muhamed Filipovic was in Yugoslavia all the time, was he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was he persecuted for his opinions by the Communist authorities?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not persecuted. There were some differences, but he wasn't detained or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the situation after October 1991 and about the atmosphere in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the efforts of all three sides to reach a peaceful agreement, in his book, Mr. Muhamed Filipovic, entitled "I Was Alija's Diplomat," when speaking of this specific time and those days in parliament, he says the following, and I'm asking you to say whether you agree or disagree with this view. With your permission, I'd like to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to the book of Mr. Muhamed Filipovic, "I Was Alija's Diplomat," "Alija" meaning Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's published in Sarajevo, year 2000, page 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation][As read] "In such both miserable and equally difficult situation, a conference was held in Brussels on the situation in the former Yugoslavia. At this conference, it was said that not only Slovenia and Croatia, but also the other republics of the former Yugoslavia, can perhaps leave the federal state if they carry out certain legal and political actions before that," [In English] constitutional and legal preconditions, " [Interpretation] and reach that through appropriate legal parliamentary procedure, or perhaps by way of a referendum of citizens. "They brought our people and our country into a situation with no way out, and these same people from the SDA opted for this second solution. They knew, of course, that they could not carry through a proposal on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina through legal procedure in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they could not overcome the obstacle of the constitutional obligation not to have any decision that affects the vital interests of any of the constituent peoples of the country -- can be reached by outvoting, and views on it have to be accommodated in the commission for the equality of nationalities." Mr. Tihic, do you agree with this view?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this period, from October 1991 until the 6th of April, 1992, did you, as a member of the Main Board of the SDA, at certain meetings discuss the subject matter involving a peaceful settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we had two or three sessions at that time, and reports were always presented about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; and people went to Lisbon, and various delegations came from there and discussions were held, and an effort was always made to try to preserve Yugoslavia. Izetbegovic had advocated a graduated federation, anything but the break-up of Yugoslavia. Therefore, I disagree with Filipovic. I think that we made every effort to preserve Yugoslavia, and Izetbegovic personally did as well. Because we simply knew that we did not have the strength or the weapons and that we were not prepared for war.
