And there were Muslims in other republics, in Sandzak and elsewhere, so we did not welcome this with open arms, especially not as Filipovic presented it. But we did not want to remain alone in this rump Yugoslavia without Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood you, at the Main Board there were a few debates about the efforts made by the International Community and the participation of the delegation of the SDA in the peace process; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally attend these meetings of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there were sessions of the Main Board, I was present at all sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with some of the basic principles, since you've mentioned this Lisbon agreement. You probably remember what this was about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to explain to us, to the best of your recollections, the things that you remember and the extent to which you remember them so that we would avoid further debates.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time Izetbegovic and Mahmut Cehajic, when they came from Lisbon - I don't know who else was there --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but could you please just slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They informed the Main Board about this, that proposals were being put forth in which the national ethnic criterion was of paramount importance in rearranging Bosnia-Herzegovina and creating these national territories. At that time we at the Main Board were against this, because we thought that Bosnia was so intertwined that it was difficult to create ethnically pure areas. And in Lisbon, they took as a point of departure that if a particular ethnic group of people was the majority in, say, a municipality - they didn't call them entities or cantons - that this would be the territory of that people, that population. We at the Main Board were not in favour of this kind of ethnic division then. We thought that the basis for reorganising Bosnia-Herzegovina were supposed to be historical, geographical, and economic criteria, and then ultimately the ethnic criterion as well, but it could not be done only on the basis of the ethnic criterion. Well, had we known that there would be a war after that, perhaps things would be viewed differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. I have before me a text of the Lisbon agreement, or better known as Cutilliero's plan, and in principle what you say is correct. There were three constituents within Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The decisions were reached with a three-quarter majority vote?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Mr. Usher, please, I need your assistance. Your Honours, I have a map of this Lisbon Agreement, so maybe it will be appropriate for witness just to make a short comment about the territories according to that map, because we are entering in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering whether the Prosecution has a copy. MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can get first -- I mean, it's not for the evidence, not for ID number. It's simply just a kind of illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. But it's being referred to, it's being shown to the witness, and the witness is going to answer some questions, so it is part of the evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: It has to be marked, I agree. We can't just have documents floating about without being identified. At the very least, it's got to be marked - I would insist on that - before the witness comments on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I wanted to find out whether the Prosecution has a copy. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got a copy now. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's a problem with the Defence. We have been through this so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then you withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw. It's no problem. We shall introduce that during the expert -- testimony of the expert witness. It's no problem, Your Honour. It's okay. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Your Honour, I have with me a piece of paper which I have some maybe - maybe I'm wrong - some idea that it was made by Mr. Tihic. I wasn't in situation to verify that issue. I would like to show this document to Mr. Tihic and simply he will say, "This is my document," or, "It is not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is it? What's the title?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: These are, I think, minutes of the -- I cannot read this handwriting. It's minutes of a session of original board of SDA in Doboj, of 18 February, 1992, just for the identification to see whether he recognised this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. We are back again. Does the Prosecution have a copy? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is a criminal trial, Mr. Pantelic. This is a criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you want to see the witness outside the proceedings, you are entitled to do that, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, and in the presence of the Prosecution, if you just want him to assist you in another way, but certainly this is a criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes of course. I don't know actually from where, and maybe he will say, "No it is not my" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He is not going to be shown that document, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You don't even know it yourself, so the Prosecution have not got a copy, and you don't seem to be willing to give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I wasn't sure that that was his copy, so I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, even if you're not sure, if you have a document which you think is important to your case, the case for your client, you give a copy to the Prosecution. If it's in Serbo-Croat, get it translated. If it's taking too long, give a copy in Serbo-Croat to the Prosecution. Maybe they can have a translation. What is important is that they have a document before it is shown to the witness in court, so that they can make their own investigations and make a stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct. If he will say that this is his handwriting, then I will go and have a copy, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He is not going to be shown a document which the Defence is not willing to give to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Tihic, I really don't know whether this is your document or not and we can't ascertain it at this point. Would you be so kind as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are asking him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking him about the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but show the copy to the Prosecution, please. The Prosecution will have -- may need to re-examine the witness on the contents of that document. How do they verify it? What is your problem? Because you can just put the questions to him without referring to the document, if you want, if there is a meeting you want him to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But I cannot discuss it. I don't know if he was the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And they are in Serbo-Croat again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But he can read if he recognise that. That's the problem. I cannot read, Your Honour, because it's illegible, absolutely illegible. So you know how it works. For identification purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me hear from the Prosecution first. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I would object to the use of this document. It's -- I haven't -- I didn't object to the use of the gazettes and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, even though they were untranslated. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps that was a risky move, I don't know, but this is an altogether different class of document. It's hand-written, I don't know what it says, I've never seen it before, and even if it is marked for identification, by the time it comes for me to stand up tomorrow morning and start re-examining, I won't be in any more enlightened position. In practical terms I'm not going to be able to do that or investigate it, so from that point of view, it shouldn't even be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: In my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It won't be shown to the witness. It won't be used in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the Defence counsel just has to comply with procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with this approach, and I'm happy to provide the Prosecution with a copy of this manuscript, and then they can confer with the witness and then see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They have looked at it, and they say it's illegible. It's in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree. Mr. Usher, please, could you give this copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it another copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's another copy. Give me the other ones, because you have one, Mr. di Fazio, and I give -- that copy also, because I have enough copies for the purposes of the identification. So tomorrow they will check with Mr. Tihic and they will say whether it's his writing or not, and then we shall proceed on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Translation? Maybe he can read. Assuming that that's his document, he can read, then our interpreters can give us the exact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Fine. In that case, then, we will postpone dealing with this document until the Prosecution have got their instructions, and I will allow the Prosecution leave to consult with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Absolutely. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then tomorrow morning, they can tell the Chamber what their stand is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No objections from Defence. Thank you, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honour please, of course, I'm happy to do that and to do our best to try and ascertain the mystery that lies behind this document. But whether or not we can do that before tomorrow morning and when we start re-examination is another issue. I'll do -- the Prosecution will do its level best but -- I know that we face practical problems with this sort of thing once we leave this courtroom. So it's not impossible but there are difficulties from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to deal with that towards the end because I wanted to find out how long Mr. Pantelic thinks he still needs to complete cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. My rough estimation would be, Your Honours -- let's say, first, I was of impression that we are going to work today according to the yesterday's schedule, until 6.30 p.m., something like that, so I made a short conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Today we are adjourning at 1715, so after that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would say, to do my best, until lunch break tomorrow. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You asked for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really a crucial issue and matter. It's a unique situation to have such a nice gentleman here and have him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Fine. We shall see how far we shall go because we have to allow Prosecution time to see the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course. And that brings me to another question with your permission, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, you arrived here on Monday, I believe?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since Monday to the present day, have you met with any of the representatives of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Didn't you see any of them when you were here and then went to Sarajevo, any of the representatives?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, that's interesting, because I gave some documents to the Prosecution seven days ago, because I was intending to use it during your cross-examination, but they didn't contact you about that, did they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, then, I apologise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Did those documents include these ones you are trying to show the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: These are different documents, yes, so I simply thought maybe they were in contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, maybe you can proceed on other points and see how far we go. Then we will see what time to allow the Prosecution to meet with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They have to deal with that before you complete your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, we are now going to talk about cooperation between the SDA and the HDZ and the SDS at a local level in political life. I have a text of your very fresh recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, I have B/C/S version of his work. So maybe, in order to facilitate communication with the witness, when I'm referring to certain parts or gist of this work, maybe I can give a copy on B/C/S language so that I can easily check with the witness, like we doing with witness statements and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's memoirs from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you write your memoirs? What year was that, 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think this is the material that the Prosecution was prohibited from using in its examination-in-chief of this particular witness. I think they are the memoirs of Mr. Tihic, and it's quite unfair, of course, for the -- for this material to be used by the Defence when the Prosecution hasn't been entitled to ask any of its questions in examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is it? MR. DI FAZIO: It's the book, I think, the memoirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the usher please collect the document and show the Prosecution so that we can verify?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this, Your Honour. The Defence actually got this material from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want them to -- you've got it and see whether it's the same copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's the same copy. I have a B/C/S version and I have an English version here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are they the same? MR. DI FAZIO: It's the memoirs all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'll just quote -- I'm very grateful to my colleague Ms. Reidy for her use of this computer, and this is what was said at the time of the objection. "Mr. Pantelic: Madam President, Your Honours, we strongly object to this proposal from our learned colleagues from the Prosecution on the basis that we act here according to the rules. We have very precise and stringent rules. Our colleagues from the Prosecution filed a list of exhibits and therefore notified the Defence about the list, exact list of exhibits, and to some extent they gave us information about, I would say, evidence framework for these proceedings."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Slow down. MR. DI FAZIO: "And due to that fact, I think if this application would be granted, then we are entering into an area of legal insecurity because we have very precise rules." And the objection was -- I don't need to quote any further but that -- the objection was upheld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: These are the memoirs where it was established that they weren't notes made contemporaneously. MR. DI FAZIO: That's exactly right. They are classic memoirs. They are memoirs written -- as one reads them, it looks like a book. Whether one calls it a book or memoirs is neither here nor there, but they are precisely and exactly the same material that was objected to by the Defence, and from my recollection, all of the defendants joined in the objection. And now, use is being sought to be made of that. Now, that's unfair, in the Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very simple. It's very simple situation. First of all, I am not of intention to tender this material as exhibits. Not at all. I, in order to facilitate this communication with the witness, would like to have in front of him his papers and to go through the questions and make some comments. So it is not a question, it is not an issue here, that I am going to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just to let you pause for breath for one second. I do have the transcript in front of me dealing with this issue, pages 1491 and onwards for a few pages, and I see, first of all, that the memoirs were actually prepared in 1995, according to our transcript, and my colleague, Judge Singh, asked a couple of questions to Mr. di Fazio concerning basically if there is any material contained in those memoirs, he asked the Prosecution why, basically, you wouldn't put it to the witness without looking at the diary. And likewise our Presiding Judge, Judge Mumba, basically said that the rule is where the witness is available, get the evidence from the witness viva voce, and I think that's the position where we ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in addition, Your Honours, if you allow me, as I said, we, in order to facilitate this communication, should have certain paper, because there are many events, so this witness can maybe be in good position to give some comments. That's the first thing. Another thing is that the Defence is, I think, perfectly entitled to use all materials and documents previously provided by the Prosecution in the process of discovery. That's a bottom line. This is the general principle of fairness of trial so that Defence is entitled to use all materials. Third point is that I'm acting on behalf of Mr. Blagoje Simic, and we -- I, as Defence, I don't have any relation with the Prosecutor with regard to the reciprocal discovery. So they, in process of discovery, are entitled to give me a certain number of documents, and also me. So I am a little bit, you know, aside of this general, I would say, relations between Prosecutor and Defence. In short, I think - and I'm speaking on behalf of my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic - I think that Defence for Blagoje Simic is entitled to use these notes, book, memoirs, whatever it is, during the cross-examination and during the preparation of the defence of my client. That would be my submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, with respect, the memoirs are really in no different position from a statement or a writing or a previous utterance by this witness, just as if the OTP had gone to him in 1995 and asked him to write a hundred-page book of his recollections of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Judge Williams rightly pointed out, with respect, that the preference of the Chamber is, and the rule of the Chamber is, that the primary source of evidence from a witness is viva voce evidence, and that's a familiar concept in many, many jurisdictions. If Mr. Pantelic wants to put extracts from the memoirs to the witness in order to prove that he is now making inconsistent statements, that's another matter altogether. That's another matter altogether. He can use the memoirs as if they were a statement, and I would have no objection. If Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My situation -- MR. DI FAZIO: And I've got no problem with that, but tendering the book into evidence is not right, in the Prosecution's submission, and is not the right approach. The right approach for Mr. Pantelic would be to put his proposition that he wants Mr. Tihic to agree with, and if Mr. Tihic agrees with his proposition, all well and good. If Mr. Tihic says something that Mr. Pantelic considers is inconsistent with what he has placed in his memoirs or written in his memoirs back in 1995, then Mr. Pantelic can put that part of the memoirs to the witness. But that's the extent of the use of the memoirs, that should be permitted, in the Prosecution's submission. If Mr. Pantelic approaches these memoirs in much the same way as a statement, then we won't get into this sort of difficulty, but simply presenting it to the witness, and/or tendering it, is not, in the Prosecution's submission, an acceptable way to approach the evidence of this witness. The first and primary source is what Mr. Tihic says, and if Mr. Pantelic wants to say, "Well, no. You've said something different on a previous occasion," he can identify that previous occasion to the witness and ask the witness to comment. And in the Prosecution's submission, that is the way the matter should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We don't have any dispute. That was my -- I don't want to tender it into evidence, no. Secondly, in order to facilitate communication with the witness with regard to certain events, just for a clarification, nothing more, and then he will give his oral answer. That's it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So if you ask him the questions, if you put the extracts --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- the memoirs to him, that would be okay. So you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was my intention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can deal with that tomorrow. I wanted to excuse -- to allow the witness to leave the courtroom so that we can discuss a point on which we don't seem to be settled, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the witness can be escorted out. We will proceed tomorrow at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to find out from the Prosecution about the possible next witness. I had given instructions to the legal officer to convey the Chamber's view about the witnesses dealing with Mr. Simic's involvement, so we would like to know what your intentions are. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. The next witness that the Prosecution proposes to call is Mr. Esad Dagovic. We've been in communication with him. He's arriving here this evening. My colleague, Mr. Weiner, who you can see is absent, is hopefully going to proof him tonight and tomorrow morning, and he should be ready to proceed as the next witness. And given the fact that Mr. Pantelic is going to use part of tomorrow morning, at least, for continued cross-examination, I'm hopeful that his proofing process will be completed and so that matters should proceed smoothly from there. You mentioned a witness dealing directly with Mr. Milan Simic. This witness does not deal directly with Mr. Milan Simic. The remaining witness who will deal with the particular factual episode, the issue in the primary school, is a gentleman named Perica Misic, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Can we deal with the witness who is ready, available, for instance, tomorrow afternoon. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. In that case, I can tell you that Esad Dagovic is going to be the next witness. The Defence know about that. They've told me they agree with that. In fact, they told me they preferred that to calling the expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The other one. MR. DI FAZIO: -- the demographics expert, Ewa Tabeau. So they've been accommodated in that respect, and that's what we propose to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If that is agreed with the Defence on the next witness, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Everything is fine with the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is fine. So the other matters are these -- I think I told the counsel for Mr. Simo Zaric about the offloading from the Internet and also making sure that that is the correct text, because it's your case. Like I said, you have the obligation to hand it in. We are remaining with, I think, three matters to be decided: the complaint about the witness' contact; and the document Variant B, whether or not it should be admitted; and the motion to the Chamber from the Defence that it should visit Bosanski Samac. Yes. The two, the first two, will be decided before Friday so that the parties have the recess to deal with whatever has to be dealt with, and the other one we think will go halfway, maybe towards the end of the Prosecution case, to see how much of the evidence may require onsite inspection. I would also take this opportunity to inform the parties that during the recess, please let's get the documents issue sorted out: Translations; if not possible, the copies be given to the Prosecution. It is very important for the trial to be fair, even to the Prosecution, in as far as cross-examination is concerned, so that we don't have these problems during trial time and we can use trial time as much as possible to receive evidence from the witnesses. We'll adjourn, unless there are any -- some other matters. Because tomorrow we are going back to our schedule, 0930 hours to 1300 hours, and then, in the afternoon, 1530 to 1700 hours. I haven't forgotten giving the Prosecution time for Mr. Tihic. Yes, we'll keep that in mind. We'll see how the cross-examination will continue in the morning. But I'm sure they can try to see if they can get some maybe translation from your office. Not the official translation; just to assist you while you are waiting for proofing, to get instructions on the document. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. You mean the document that was revealed this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the one -- MR. DI FAZIO: Right. Yes. I don't think that will be a problem. I think that if we can't do it tonight, we'll certainly be able to do it early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I believe my colleague has a comment to make in respect of the Variant A and B issue, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. What I've understood you to say is that you would be ruling on the matter by the time the Court rises for recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Your Honour Judge Singh had made a suggestion that we submit a -- there have been inter parte steps between us and Defence on this matter already, and Mr. Singh -- Your Honour Judge Singh suggested that we submit a witness summary as to who we might call on that. The witness summary is, as such, prepared. The person that we would consider most appropriate to call is on mission and has been on mission for a while, because of many other things which are going on in this Tribunal, isn't due back on Sunday. Before Your Honours rule on that, I don't know whether you would be interested in seeing the witness summary, and if so, I can try tomorrow, through secure fax, to contact the witness, have him agree or not agree with the summary, and then submit it perhaps by close of tomorrow or Friday morning. But I'd just -- I guess I just want to make clear on the record that before you rule on that matter, there is an outstanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Matter to be submitted by the Prosecution. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I -- Ms. Reidy has put the situation to you very clearly. Just to be absolutely clear, though, the Prosecution position is that it does wish to provide you with that evidence as to the source of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It's the Prosecution's submission that it's crucial, really, to its -- to the admission of this document, and we would go further and say rather than simply respond to an invitation from the Chamber, our position is that we do wish to put this material before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the Trial Chamber. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Before I let you speak, Ms. Baen, I was trying to find also whether the document which was solicited from Trial Chamber I has been released to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can hear from the Registry assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have it here in the courtroom to be distributed, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- to the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that will be done after we have risen. So we will rise and we will continue our proceedings tomorrow morning at -- I'm sorry, Ms. Baen. I forgot about you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That tends to happen to me, actually, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You should sit right in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I like to hide behind the pole, though, just for strategic reasons. My understanding when we had this conversation about the Variant A, B document, when Judge Singh raised this issue, is that we were going to receive the information from the Prosecutors as to the source of this document, which is exactly what they say they have now, is this witness statement, and so we sure would like to have a copy of that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see, and then you may wish to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Then we can postpone it until we get the documents from the Prosecution, and they should serve them on the Defence as well. Then we can deal with it perhaps after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll adjourn and continue tomorrow our proceedings at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
